title: Empires, Trade and Nations · Episode 2
chapters: Bismarck and the making of Germany
The Panama Canal: cutting a continent in two

units.t: Empires, Trade and Nations. Episode two.
In this episode: Meiji Japan: the great makeover, Bismarck and the making of Germany and The Panama Canal: cutting a continent in two.
Part one. Meiji Japan: the great makeover.
In about forty years, Japan went from a closed realm of samurai and shoguns to an industrial power that defeated a European empire.
How did it happen so fast?
A closed country opens.
In the early 1600s the Tokugawa family unified Japan and ruled as shoguns, military leaders who held real power while the emperor lived in ceremonial seclusion at Kyoto.
Fearing missionaries and European influence, they restricted foreign contact.
Japanese were generally forbidden to travel abroad, and European trade was limited to the Dutch on Dejima, a small island in Nagasaki harbour.
Japan was not frozen: Edo, now Tokyo, grew huge, literacy was high and the arts flourished.
But its rulers did not grasp how fast Western industry was changing.
In July 1853 four American ships under Commodore Perry steamed into Edo Bay, two of them smoking steamers the Japanese called black ships.
Perry demanded open ports.
The shogunate signed the Treaty of Kanagawa in 1854, then 'unequal treaties' fixing low tariffs and letting foreigners be tried in their own courts.
Restoration and the samurai.
Many Japanese were humiliated.
Ambitious samurai from Satsuma and Choshu plotted against the Tokugawa under the slogan 'revere the emperor, expel the barbarians'.
Clashes with Western warships taught them expelling foreigners was impossible, so Japan would have to learn from the West.
The last shogun gave up power, and after a short civil war the emperor was declared restored.
He was a teenager named Mutsuhito, and his reign took the name Meiji, meaning 'enlightened rule'.
Edo was renamed Tokyo, 'eastern capital'.
The new leaders moved fast.
In 1871 they replaced feudal domains with prefectures and began cutting samurai stipends.
A conscript army replaced the samurai monopoly on fighting, and public sword-wearing was largely banned in 1876.
In 1877 the Satsuma Rebellion, led by Saigo Takamori, was crushed by the conscript army.
Learning from the world.
In 1871 the Iwakura Mission, a large government delegation, set off to tour the United States and Europe for well over a year.
It visited factories, schools, parliaments, shipyards and prisons, taking careful notes.

Japan then borrowed selectively: a navy modelled on Britain's, an army influenced first by France and later by Germany, legal codes drawing on French and German law, and a school system with ideas from several countries.
The government hired thousands of foreign experts, then gradually replaced them with Japanese graduates.
One slogan captured the goal: 'rich country, strong army'.
Another described Japanese spirit with Western techniques.
Even the calendar changed, as Japan adopted the Western solar calendar from 1873.
Railways, silk and a constitution.
Japan's first railway, between Tokyo and Yokohama, opened in 1872.
The government built model factories, including a large silk mill at Tomioka, then sold many enterprises cheaply to private businesses.
This helped create powerful family conglomerates called zaibatsu, such as Mitsubishi and Mitsui.
Silk exports earned the foreign currency needed for machinery and warships.
Primary schooling became compulsory.
In 1889 the emperor granted a written constitution, influenced by Prussia's, which created an elected parliament called the Diet.
Voting was limited to a small minority of wealthy men, and the emperor was declared sacred and inviolable.
Even so, Japan became the first East Asian nation with a Western-style constitution.
Power and a warning.
Japan's transformation was tested in war.
It defeated China in 1894 to 1895 and took Taiwan as a colony.
In 1904 to 1905 it shocked the world by defeating Russia on land and at sea, the first time in modern history that an Asian nation beat a European great power in a major war.
It also ended foreign extraterritoriality, agreed in 1894, and regained full control of its tariffs in 1911.
When the Meiji emperor died in 1912, Japan was an industrial and colonial power that had annexed Korea in 1910.
The era is often held up as a model of rapid modernisation.
But the same drive for national strength, and the army's growing political power, helped set Japan on a path towards militarism, expansion in Asia and, eventually, the Pacific War.
The key idea: After over two centuries of seclusion, American warships in 1853 forced Japan to open up and exposed the shogunate's weakness.
Part two. Bismarck and the making of Germany.
In 1860 there was no country called Germany, just dozens of separate states.
Eleven years later a German empire was proclaimed in a French palace, built by one man's three wars.
Blood and iron.
After 1815 the German lands formed a loose Confederation of 39 states, from great powers like Austria and Prussia to tiny free cities like Hamburg.
Prussia grew rich through industry and the Zollverein, a customs union that excluded Austria.
In 1848 an elected parliament in Frankfurt tried to unite Germany, and failed.
In 1862 King Wilhelm I was stuck in a fight with parliament over funding for a bigger army.
He appointed Otto von Bismarck, a ruthless Junker diplomat, who simply carried on collecting taxes without approval.
He declared that the great questions of the day would be decided not by speeches and majority votes, but by iron and blood.
The phrase came to define his career.
Three wars in seven years.
Bismarck's genius lay in fighting one enemy at a time, ensuring no other power joined in.
In 1864 Prussia and Austria together defeated Denmark over Schleswig and Holstein.
Bismarck then used disputes over running those duchies to provoke Austria.
In 1866 the Prussian army, using railways, telegraphs and fast-firing breech-loading rifles, crushed Austria at Königgrätz in a war lasting only weeks.
Bismarck insisted on mild terms so Austria would not seek revenge, but it was pushed out of German affairs.
Prussia annexed several states and formed the North German Confederation.
Only the southern states, including Bavaria, remained outside.
Bismarck believed a war with France would bring them in.
The Ems Telegram and Versailles.
In 1870 a relative of the Prussian king was offered the Spanish throne.
France protested and it was withdrawn, but France pressed further, demanding at Ems a promise it would never be renewed.
Wilhelm politely declined and telegraphed Bismarck.
Bismarck shortened the message so the king seemed to have curtly snubbed the ambassador.
The French public was outraged and France declared war, appearing the aggressor.
The southern states, bound by defensive alliances, joined Prussia.
At Sedan Napoleon III was captured.
On 18 January 1871, with Paris besieged, Wilhelm I was proclaimed Kaiser in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, a deliberate humiliation.
France paid an indemnity and gave up Alsace and much of Lorraine.
Bismarck at home.
As chancellor, Bismarck saw enemies of the new empire everywhere.
In the 1870s he waged the Kulturkampf against the power of the Catholic Church, which backfired by strengthening Catholic political loyalty.
He then turned on the socialist movement, banning its organisations from 1878.
Yet alongside repression came a remarkable innovation.
To win workers away from socialism, he introduced national health insurance in 1883, accident insurance in 1884, and old age and disability pensions in 1889.
Workers, employers and the state shared the costs.
It was the first system of its kind in the world and became a model for many other countries.
His motives were conservative, but the legacy proved lasting.
The juggler and his fall.
After 1871 Bismarck declared Germany satisfied.
His aim was to prevent a war that could destroy what he had built, especially a two-front war against France and Russia.

He presented himself as an honest broker at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, and wove a network of treaties: the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879, later the Triple Alliance with Italy, and a secret Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1887.
In 1888 the young Wilhelm II came to the throne and clashed with the old chancellor, who was forced to resign in 1890.
The treaty with Russia was not renewed, and Russia soon allied with France.
The isolation Bismarck feared was beginning to take shape, setting the stage for 1914.
The key idea: Bismarck argued that Germany would be united by force rather than speeches and votes, the supposed mistake of 1848.
Part three. The Panama Canal: cutting a continent in two.
For centuries people dreamed of a shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific.
The first attempt ended in disaster.
The second succeeded only after doctors worked out what was really killing the workers.
The dream, the failure.
Panama is a narrow strip of land, at its slimmest under 80 kilometres wide.
A ship sailing from New York to San Francisco had to go around Cape Horn, a voyage of more than 20,000 kilometres.
A canal would cut roughly 13,000 kilometres from it.
In 1881 a French company led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, hero of the Suez Canal, began digging.
He insisted on a sea-level canal with no locks.
But Panama was nothing like flat Egyptian desert: mountains, landslides, heavy rains and the flooding Chagres River defeated the plan.
Yellow fever and malaria killed workers in huge numbers, around 20,000 during the French years, many of them Caribbean labourers.
By 1889 the company was bankrupt, and the half-dug ditches were left to the jungle.
America steps in.
At the start of the twentieth century, the United States wanted a canal for trade and to move its navy quickly between oceans.
President Theodore Roosevelt bought the French company's assets, but Colombia, which then ruled Panama, rejected the treaty terms.
In November 1903 a revolt in Panama declared independence, and US warships made sure Colombian troops could not land to stop it.

Within about two weeks the new government's representative, a Frenchman named Philippe Bunau-Varilla, signed a treaty giving the United States control of a Canal Zone across the country, in perpetuity.
Many Panamanians resented the deal from the start, and it became a source of tension in Latin America for decades.
Defeating the mosquito.
Work began in 1904, and at first yellow fever returned and workers fled.
The breakthrough came from medicine.
Building on Carlos Finlay's theory and Walter Reed's experiments in Cuba, doctors had confirmed that yellow fever was spread by mosquitoes, while malaria was carried by a different mosquito.
Doctor William Gorgas, the chief sanitary officer, launched a vast campaign.
Teams drained swamps, spread oil on standing water, fumigated buildings, screened windows and installed piped water so people no longer stored it in open barrels.
By 1906 yellow fever had been eliminated from the zone, and malaria deaths fell sharply.
It was one of the great public health victories in history, and without it the canal would likely have failed again.
Locks, lake, workers.
Chief engineers John Stevens and later George Goethals abandoned the sea-level idea.
They dammed the Chagres River at Gatun, creating then the largest artificial lake in the world.
Ships climb through giant locks, cross the lake about 26 metres above sea level, then descend through more locks.
The hardest work was the Culebra Cut through the mountainous spine of the isthmus, where landslides repeatedly buried months of digging.
On 15 August 1914 the cargo ship SS Ancon made the first official transit.
Most labour came from the Caribbean, especially Barbados and Jamaica, doing the most dangerous jobs.
White Americans were paid in gold, most other workers in silver, with poorer housing and food.
Over 5,000 workers died in the American years.
Handing back the canal.
Resentment of the Canal Zone, a slice of US-run territory cutting through the middle of Panama, grew through the twentieth century.
In 1964 riots over flying the Panamanian flag in the zone left more than twenty people dead.
In 1977 US President Jimmy Carter and Panama's leader Omar Torrijos signed treaties to transfer the canal.
On 31 December 1999 Panama took full control.
Since then it has run the canal profitably and opened larger locks in 2016 to take bigger ships.
The canal still depends on rain to fill Gatun Lake, and in 2023 a severe drought forced limits on the number of ships that could pass, a reminder that even great engineering relies on nature.
The key idea: A canal would save around 13,000 kilometres of sailing, but the first attempt failed because of terrain, a flawed design and disease.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did Perry's 1853 visit expose the shogunate's weakness?
Answer. It showed the shogun could not resist foreign warships.
Question two. What did Bismarck mean by ‘iron and blood’?
Answer. That force, not votes, would settle it.
Question three. Why did the French effort to build the canal fail?
Answer. Landslides, floods and fever overwhelmed it.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
